title: Dynamics & Momentum
description: Hooke's law and the spring constant, F = ma, circular motion, momentum, impulse and the conservation of momentum in one dimension — the Extended-tier mechanics of IGCSE Physics 0625.

notes.heading: Hooke's Law: F = kx
notes.body:
📌 Definition
Below its **limit of proportionality**, the force needed to stretch a spring is directly proportional to the extension:
$$F = kx$$
where $x$ is the extension (stretched length − original length, in metres) and $k$ is the **spring constant**, in N/m. A larger $k$ means a STIFFER spring — more force per metre of extension.

🔑 How it works
The spring constant is the gradient of the load-extension graph's straight-line section. Past the limit of proportionality the graph curves, $F = kx$ no longer holds, and the spring may be permanently stretched.

💡 Worked Example
A force of $6$ N extends a spring by $0.03$ m:
$$k = \dfrac{F}{x} = \dfrac{6}{0.03} = 200\text{ N/m}$$
Conversely, a force of $7$ N on a spring with $k = 50\text{ N/m}$ extends it by $x = \dfrac{F}{k} = \dfrac{7}{50} = 0.14\text{ m} = 14$ cm.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Substituting the extension in centimetres. $k$ is in N/m, so convert $x$ to metres first — $3$ cm is $0.03$ m.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• $F = kx$ holds ONLY below the limit of proportionality.
• Extension, not total length, goes into the equation.

notes.heading: Newton's Second Law: F = ma
notes.body:
📌 Definition
The acceleration of an object is proportional to the resultant force on it and inversely proportional to its mass:
$$F = ma$$
$F$ in newtons, $m$ in kilograms, $a$ in m/s². $F$ is the RESULTANT force — the single force equivalent to everything acting.

🔑 How it works
The same force accelerates a light object more than a heavy one; the same object accelerates more under a bigger force. If forces partly cancel, subtract first, then apply $F = ma$ to the resultant.

💡 Worked Example
An $800$ kg car speeds up from $10\text{ m/s}$ to $22\text{ m/s}$ in $4$ s. First the acceleration: $a = \dfrac{22 - 10}{4} = 3\text{ m/s}^2$. Then the force: $F = ma = 800 \times 3 = 2400$ N.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Applying $F = ma$ to a single force when others act. If an engine provides $3000$ N against $600$ N of drag, the resultant is $2400$ N — and $2400$ N is what goes into $F = ma$.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Resultant force → acceleration. Zero resultant → zero acceleration (Newton's first law).
• Weight is just $F = ma$ with $a = g$: $W = mg$.

notes.heading: Circular Motion
notes.body:
📌 The key idea
An object moving in a circle at CONSTANT SPEED is still accelerating, because its velocity — a vector — is changing direction continuously. Acceleration requires a resultant force, so circular motion always needs an inward force.

🔑 How it works
The force acts PERPENDICULAR to the motion, towards the centre of the circle (it is called a centripetal force, though it is always provided by something real): gravity for a satellite or the Moon, friction between tyres and road for a cornering car, tension in the string for a whirled ball. The force changes the DIRECTION of the velocity, not its size.

🔑 Qualitative dependencies (exam favourites)
The force needed is GREATER for: a greater mass, a greater speed, or a SMALLER radius (a tighter circle). This is why a car can skid off a bend taken too fast, and why passengers feel 'thrown outwards' — in reality their bodies try to keep going straight while the car turns.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Claiming an outward 'centrifugal force' pushes the object. There is no outward force on the circling object — if the string breaks, the ball flies off along a TANGENT, continuing in the direction it was moving at that instant (Newton's first law).

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Constant speed ≠ constant velocity when the direction changes.
• The force points to the centre; the object would fly off tangentially without it.

notes.heading: Momentum: p = mv
notes.body:
📌 Definition
$$\text{momentum} = \text{mass} \times \text{velocity} \qquad p = mv$$
Unit: kg·m/s. Momentum is a VECTOR — it has the direction of the velocity, which makes signs matter in collision questions: choose one direction as positive and stick to it.

🔑 How it works
Momentum measures 'how much motion' something has and how hard it is to stop. A heavy lorry at walking pace has more momentum than a sprinting cyclist; a bullet is light but its enormous velocity gives it serious momentum.

💡 Worked Example
A $60$ kg runner moving at $3\text{ m/s}$ has momentum $p = 60 \times 3 = 180\text{ kg m/s}$ in the direction of running.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Using SPEED when the direction has reversed. If a ball rebounds, its velocity changes sign, and its momentum changes by MORE than the two magnitudes suggest — see the impulse note.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• $p = mv$; the unit kg·m/s is the same as N·s.
• Zero velocity → zero momentum, whatever the mass.

notes.heading: Impulse and F = Δp/Δt
notes.body:
📌 Definition
Force is the rate of change of momentum:
$$F = \dfrac{\Delta p}{\Delta t} = \dfrac{\Delta(mv)}{\Delta t} \qquad\text{so}\qquad F\Delta t = \Delta p$$
The product $F\Delta t$ is called the **impulse** — it equals the change in momentum produced.

🔑 How it works — and why it saves lives
For a FIXED change in momentum (stopping a passenger in a crash, catching a fast ball), the force is smaller when the collision takes LONGER: $F = \dfrac{\Delta p}{\Delta t}$. Crumple zones, seatbelts, airbags, crash mats and bending your knees on landing all EXTEND the impact time $\Delta t$ and so reduce the peak force.

💡 Worked Example
A $0.05$ kg ball approaches a wall at $8\text{ m/s}$ and rebounds at $6\text{ m/s}$. Taking the initial direction as positive: $\Delta p = 0.05 \times (-6 - 8) = -0.7\text{ kg m/s}$ — magnitude $0.7\text{ kg m/s}$. If the contact lasts $0.02$ s:
$$F = \dfrac{0.7}{0.02} = 35\text{ N}$$

⚠️ Common Mistake
Computing $\Delta p$ as $0.05 \times (8 - 6) = 0.1\text{ kg m/s}$. On a rebound the velocity changes sign, so the magnitudes ADD: the change is $8 - (-6) = 14\text{ m/s}$, not $2\text{ m/s}$.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Longer impact time → smaller force, same $\Delta p$.
• Rebounds: add the speeds when finding $\Delta v$.

notes.heading: Conservation of Momentum in One Dimension
notes.body:
📌 The principle
When no external resultant force acts on a system, the **total momentum before an event equals the total momentum after it**:
$$m_1 u_1 + m_2 u_2 = m_1 v_1 + m_2 v_2$$
This applies to collisions (objects hitting and sticking or bouncing) and to explosions (one object flying apart).

🔑 Two standard situations
• **Collision with sticking**: the objects move off together with one combined mass and one shared velocity.
• **Explosion from rest**: total momentum starts at zero, so the two momenta afterwards must be EQUAL in size and OPPOSITE in direction — a fired bullet and its recoiling rifle.

💡 Worked Example
A $2$ kg trolley moving at $3\text{ m/s}$ hits a stationary $1$ kg trolley and they stick together:
$$2 \times 3 + 1 \times 0 = (2 + 1) \times v \implies 6 = 3v \implies v = 2\text{ m/s}$$

💡 Worked Example 2 — recoil
A $4$ kg rifle fires a $0.02$ kg bullet at $300\text{ m/s}$. Momentum before $= 0$, so afterwards: $4 \times v + 0.02 \times 300 = 0$, giving recoil speed $v = \dfrac{6}{4} = 1.5\text{ m/s}$ backwards.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Forgetting that momentum is a vector — in an explosion the two momenta have opposite signs, which is what makes the total stay zero.

illustration.alt: Conservation of momentum: a 2 kg trolley at 3 m/s hits a stationary 1 kg trolley; they stick and move together at 2 m/s, because total momentum stays 6 kg·m/s before and after.
illustration.caption: Total momentum before = total momentum after, in collisions and in explosions.

notes.heading: Choosing the Right Equation
notes.body:
Extended mechanics questions reward recognising WHICH relationship applies. Use this decision guide.

🔑 Match the clue to the tool
• **A spring, with load and extension** → $F = kx$ (below the limit of proportionality).
• **Mass and acceleration, or a force changing a speed** → $F = ma$, finding $a = \dfrac{v - u}{t}$ first if speeds and a time are given.
• **A collision or explosion, masses and velocities** → conservation of momentum, $m_1 u_1 + m_2 u_2 = m_1 v_1 + m_2 v_2$.
• **A force acting for a stated TIME, or an impact time** → impulse, $F\Delta t = \Delta(mv)$.
• **Circular motion** → qualitative: resultant force towards the centre; more force for more mass, more speed, tighter radius.

💡 Worked Example
'A $0.5$ kg ball at rest is struck by a bat with an average force of $60$ N for $0.2$ s. Find its final speed.' The force-and-time clue says impulse: $\Delta p = 60 \times 0.2 = 12\text{ kg m/s}$, so $v = \dfrac{12}{0.5} = 24\text{ m/s}$.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Reaching for $F = ma$ when the question gives an impact time rather than an acceleration. Force × time gives the momentum change directly — no acceleration needed.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Write down what is GIVEN and what is ASKED; the equation that connects them is usually unique.
• Momentum questions always need a chosen positive direction — state it.

flashcards.definition: The stiffness of a spring: the force per unit extension in F = kx, measured in N/m. Found from the gradient of the load-extension graph.
flashcards.example: 6 N producing 0.03 m of extension means k = 200 N/m.

flashcards.definition: The point beyond which extension is no longer proportional to load — the load-extension graph stops being straight and F = kx no longer applies.
flashcards.example: Below the limit, doubling the load doubles the extension; above it, a small extra load stretches the spring far more.

flashcards.definition: Resultant force = mass x acceleration: F = ma, with F in N, m in kg and a in m/s².
flashcards.example: 2400 N on 800 kg produces an acceleration of 3 m/s².

flashcards.definition: The single force equivalent to all forces acting; only the RESULTANT goes into F = ma.
flashcards.example: 3000 N of thrust against 600 N of drag gives a resultant of 2400 N.

flashcards.definition: An object moving in a circle needs a resultant force directed towards the centre of the circle (a centripetal force), perpendicular to its motion.
flashcards.example: Tension in the string keeps a whirled ball circling; cut the string and it flies off along a tangent.

flashcards.definition: Velocity is a vector: at constant speed in a circle the direction changes continuously, so the velocity — and hence the momentum — is changing.
flashcards.example: The Moon at steady orbital speed is still accelerating towards the Earth.

flashcards.definition: Mass x velocity: p = mv. A vector, in kg·m/s (equivalent to N·s).
flashcards.example: A 60 kg runner at 3 m/s has 180 kg·m/s of momentum.

flashcards.definition: Momentum has the direction of the velocity: choose a positive direction and give reverse motion a negative sign.
flashcards.example: A ball rebounding at 6 m/s after approaching at 8 m/s changes velocity by 14 m/s, not 2 m/s.

flashcards.definition: Force x time for which it acts: F x delta-t = change in momentum, in N·s (= kg·m/s).
flashcards.example: 60 N applied for 0.2 s gives a momentum change of 12 kg·m/s.

flashcards.definition: Force equals the rate of change of momentum. For a fixed momentum change, a longer impact time means a smaller force.
flashcards.example: Crumple zones lengthen a crash's impact time, reducing the force on passengers.

flashcards.definition: With no external resultant force, total momentum before an event equals total momentum after — for collisions and explosions in one dimension.
flashcards.example: 2 kg at 3 m/s sticking to a stationary 1 kg trolley: 6 = 3v, so v = 2 m/s.

flashcards.definition: An explosion from rest keeps total momentum at zero: the two parts fly off with equal and opposite momenta.
flashcards.example: A 4 kg rifle firing a 0.02 kg bullet at 300 m/s recoils at 1.5 m/s.

questions.explanation: Momentum is mass multiplied by velocity, $p = mv$. $\dfrac{1}{2}mv^2$ is kinetic energy — a different quantity with different units.

questions.stem: A $60$ kg runner moves at $3\text{ m/s}$. What is her momentum?
questions.explanation: $p = mv = 60 \times 3 = 180\text{ kg m/s}$ in the direction of running. $20\text{ kg m/s}$ comes from dividing mass by velocity, and the unit is kg·m/s — no squared metres.

questions.stem: A resultant force accelerates a $5$ kg mass at $2.4\text{ m/s}^2$. What is the force?
questions.explanation: $F = ma = 5 \times 2.4 = 12$ N. $2.1$ N ($\dfrac{5}{2.4}$) and $0.48$ N ($\dfrac{2.4}{5}$) are the division done the wrong way round.

questions.stem: An $800$ kg car speeds up from $10\text{ m/s}$ to $22\text{ m/s}$ in $4.0$ s. What resultant force is needed?
questions.explanation: Two steps: $a = \dfrac{v - u}{t} = \dfrac{22 - 10}{4.0} = 3.0\text{ m/s}^2$, then $F = ma = 800 \times 3.0 = 2400$ N. $4400$ N comes from $a = \dfrac{22}{4.0}$ — using the final speed instead of the CHANGE in speed — and $9600$ N is $800 \times 12$, the speed change without dividing by time.

questions.stem: A force of $6$ N extends a spring by $3$ cm. What is the spring constant?
questions.explanation: $k = \dfrac{F}{x} = \dfrac{6}{0.03} = 200\text{ N/m}$. The extension must be converted to metres first — leaving it in centimetres gives the wrong answer $2\text{ N/m}$.

questions.stem: A spring has a spring constant of $50\text{ N/m}$. What extension does a $7$ N force produce (within the limit of proportionality)?
questions.explanation: $x = \dfrac{F}{k} = \dfrac{7}{50} = 0.14\text{ m} = 14$ cm. $0.14$ cm forgets the metres-to-centimetres conversion, and $350$ cm multiplies instead of dividing.

questions.stem: What is the limit of proportionality of a spring?
choices: The maximum load the spring can support without falling off the stand
The point at which the spring breaks
The point beyond which extension is no longer proportional to load
The load at which the spring reaches its natural length
questions.explanation: Below the limit of proportionality, extension is directly proportional to load ($F = kx$, the graph is a straight line through the origin); beyond it the graph curves and the proportional rule fails. The spring may still return to shape — the limit is not the breaking point.

questions.stem: A ball is whirled on a string in a horizontal circle. In which direction does the force keeping it in the circle act?
choices: Towards the centre of the circle
In the direction of the ball's motion
Directly outwards, away from the centre
questions.explanation: The tension acts along the string towards the centre — an inward (centripetal) resultant force is what curves the path. There is no outward force on the ball; without the string it would fly off along a tangent.

questions.stem: A satellite orbits the Earth at constant speed. Why is it nonetheless accelerating?
choices: Gravity is increasing its speed steadily
Its velocity is changing because its direction is changing, and velocity is a vector
Its mass is gradually increasing as it burns fuel
It is not accelerating — constant speed means zero acceleration
questions.explanation: Velocity has direction as well as size. Moving in a circle changes the direction continuously, so the velocity changes and the satellite accelerates towards the Earth even though the speed never changes.

questions.stem: A $0.5$ kg ball at rest is struck with an average force of $60$ N for $0.2$ s. What speed does it leave with?
questions.explanation: Impulse gives the momentum change: $\Delta p = F\Delta t = 60 \times 0.2 = 12\text{ kg m/s}$. Starting from rest, $v = \dfrac{\Delta p}{m} = \dfrac{12}{0.5} = 24\text{ m/s}$. $12\text{ m/s}$ stops halfway — that is the momentum change, not the speed.

questions.stem: A $0.05$ kg ball hits a wall at $8\text{ m/s}$ and rebounds at $6\text{ m/s}$. The contact lasts $0.02$ s. What is the average force on the ball?
questions.explanation: The velocity reverses, so the change is $8 - (-6) = 14\text{ m/s}$: $\Delta p = 0.05 \times 14 = 0.7\text{ kg m/s}$, and $F = \dfrac{0.7}{0.02} = 35$ N. $5$ N comes from the wrong change $0.05 \times (8 - 6) = 0.1\text{ kg m/s}$ — on a rebound the speeds ADD.

questions.stem: How does a crumple zone reduce the force on car passengers in a crash?
choices: It increases the time over which the momentum changes, and $F = \dfrac{\Delta p}{\Delta t}$
It absorbs the passengers' kinetic energy as heat
It reduces the momentum of the car before impact
It increases the mass of the car, spreading the force
questions.explanation: The passengers' momentum change $\Delta p$ is fixed by the crash. Crumpling lengthens the stopping time $\Delta t$, and since $F = \dfrac{\Delta p}{\Delta t}$, a larger $\Delta t$ means a smaller peak force.

questions.stem: A $2$ kg trolley moving at $3\text{ m/s}$ collides with a stationary $1$ kg trolley and they stick together. What is their shared velocity?
questions.explanation: Momentum is conserved: $2 \times 3 + 1 \times 0 = (2 + 1)v$, so $6 = 3v$ and $v = 2\text{ m/s}$. $6\text{ m/s}$ uses only the moving trolley's mass on the right-hand side.

questions.stem: A stationary $4$ kg rifle fires a $0.02$ kg bullet at $300\text{ m/s}$. What is the rifle's recoil speed?
questions.explanation: Total momentum is zero before firing, so afterwards the two momenta must be equal and opposite: $4 \times v = 0.02 \times 300 = 6\text{ kg m/s}$, giving $v = \dfrac{6}{4} = 1.5\text{ m/s}$. $6\text{ m/s}$ is the bullet's momentum, not the recoil speed.

questions.stem: What is the SI unit of momentum?
questions.explanation: Momentum $p = mv$ has units kg × m/s $=$ kg·m/s, which is identical to N·s. N/m is the spring constant's unit and J (joule) is the unit of energy.
